name: Methyl-1-testosterone (M1T)
lead: Methyl-1-testosterone (M1T, SC-11195) is a synthetic, orally active anabolic-androgenic steroid, the 17-alpha-methyl derivative of 1-testosterone. It was never marketed for medical use [1]. It appeared in the early 2000s in over-the-counter supplements aimed at bodybuilders and athletes seeking muscle size and strength [2].

Its appeal in physique circles is as an oral 'prohormone-style' product that is claimed to add muscle mass and strength, and so a more muscular, harder-looking physique. Laboratory work supports androgenic activity in cell and rat models, but no clinical trial has tested it in people for these outcomes [3].

A 2011 study identified M1T in a supplement and examined it in animal and in vitro models; a published case report links it to acute kidney injury through an interaction with ciclosporin [3][4]. The World Anti-Doping Agency lists it as prohibited [1].
infobox: None; never marketed as a drug [1]

paras: M1T is a synthetic steroid in the androgen family, described in the research literature as 17beta-hydroxy-17alpha-methyl-5alpha-androst-1-en-3-one.[3] Wikipedia classes it as an androgen receptor agonist and an anabolic-androgenic steroid, and notes that it has never been marketed as a medicine.[1] Supplement sellers marketed it to people seeking more muscle and strength.[2] No human trial has measured its effect on muscle.[3]
The compound is chemically linked to the medicine oxandrolone: Wikipedia says M1T is used as a precursor in oxandrolone synthesis.[1]

M1T is the 17-alpha-methyl derivative of 1-testosterone (dihydroboldenone) [1]. Wikipedia also notes its use as a precursor in the synthesis of oxandrolone [1]. Grokipedia, an AI-generated source treated with caution, describes the 17-alpha methyl group as a modification that helps the molecule resist hepatic breakdown when taken by mouth, and lists poor water solubility and a white crystalline appearance [2].

The 2011 characterisation study identified M1T in a supplement and tested its affinity for the androgen receptor in a yeast transactivation assay, where it behaved as a potent androgen [3]. In a rat Hershberger assay, subcutaneous M1T dose-dependently increased prostate and levator ani muscle weight; oral administration did not change those weights but stimulated prostate proliferation and modulated IGF-I and androgen receptor expression in gastrocnemius muscle [3]. Tyrosine aminotransferase expression indicated strong liver activity, much higher after oral administration [3]. Metabolites were determined by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry [3].
Later analytical work has examined phase II (conjugated) metabolites of M1T using ion-mobility mass spectrometry to improve doping-control detection [6].

The authors of the 2011 study concluded that M1T is a potent androgenic and anabolic steroid after both oral and subcutaneous administration, that it shows no selective androgen receptor modulator characteristics, and that it might exhibit liver toxicity, especially after oral administration.[3] In humans, the study confirmed M1T in urine along with its main metabolites, including 17alpha-methyl-5alpha-androst-1-ene-3alpha,17beta-diol and 17alpha-methyl-5alpha-androstane-3alpha,17beta-diol, and monitored their elimination kinetics.[3]

Grokipedia describes M1T as a 'designer steroid' that emerged in the early 2000s through its inclusion in dietary supplements for bodybuilders [2]. A 2010 Chinese study analysed an unlabelled oral product that turned out to contain M1T, which had been added to the prohibited list in 2006, and developed a urine screening method with a 2 ng/mL detection limit [5].

In the 2010 Chinese analysis, researchers used infrared, NMR, ultraviolet and mass spectroscopy to infer the unknown principal constituent of a new oral product to be M1T, and established a urine method with a detection limit of 2 ng/mL and a quantification limit of 10 ng/mL, along with an excretion curve in human urine.[5] The 2011 characterisation paper began from a supplement marketed as a dietary product that contained a rarely characterised anabolic steroid, identified as M1T.[3] Wikipedia lists M1T among substances on the World Anti-Doping Agency prohibited list, citing the 2012 list.[1]

No studies found of M1T given to people in a trial. Human evidence consists of a case report of acute kidney injury in a patient with severe atopic dermatitis taking ciclosporin who had bought M1T online [4]. Analytical studies describe detection in urine and a supplement analysis [5][6].

The case report authors note that the product can be purchased online and advise physicians to ask about supplements and consider drug interactions [4]. Grokipedia states that Health Canada issued warnings about supplements containing it and lists hepatotoxicity concerns for 17-alpha-alkylated steroids; it also reports WADA prohibition [2]. The rat study's liver-enzyme finding is consistent with those concerns in an animal model [3].

The only human clinical report is the 2013 case of acute kidney injury in a patient with severe atopic dermatitis who was taking ciclosporin and had obtained M1T online; the authors described it as the first report of this interaction and advised physicians to consider drug interactions with over-the-counter or online-purchased supplements.[4] Wikipedia categorises the compound among hepatotoxins, though its article does not discuss liver toxicity in detail.[1]

On T Nation, M1T appears mainly in lists of prohibited anabolic compounds used by natural-bodybuilding federations [7] and in potency tables comparing steroids [8]. Posters also discuss over-the-counter prohormone and designer-steroid supplements, with some noting that stores had sold them alongside SARMs [9].
Forum references are brief: lists of compounds that natural-bodybuilding federations prohibit, potency tables and recollections of designer-steroid supplements sold in shops.[7][8][9]

timeline.event: M1T appears as a designer steroid in over-the-counter bodybuilding supplements [2].
Added to prohibited doping lists, according to a Chinese urine-monitoring study [5].
Endocrine characterisation in cell and rat models published [3].
Case report of kidney injury with ciclosporin published [4].

lore.intro: M1T is discussed in lifter forums as a former OTC designer steroid and as an entry on banned-substance lists [7][8][9].

claims.claim: OTC prohormone and designer-steroid supplements are a legal shortcut to muscle
claims.believers: Some posters describe stores selling such products openly alongside SARMs, treating them as accessible options [9].
claims.experts: The 2011 study found a supplement contained an undeclared designer steroid and showed strong androgenic and liver activity in rats [3]; Health Canada has issued warnings, per Grokipedia [2].

claims.claim: M1T is highly potent by weight
claims.believers: Potency tables circulating on forums list M1T with high androgenic and anabolic ratings [8].
claims.experts: Published potency data are limited to a yeast assay and rat models; no human potency data exist [3].

card.summary: An oral designer androgen once sold as a prohormone supplement; known from animal work and a kidney-injury case report.
card.note: Prohibited in sport; case report of kidney injury with ciclosporin.

quick.overview:
M1T is an oral anabolic steroid that appeared in bodybuilding supplements in the 2000s without medical approval.

Research is limited to animal and in vitro work, analytical papers and a case report.
quick.mechanism: It is an androgen receptor agonist; a 2011 study tested receptor affinity and anabolic and androgenic potency in animals.
quick.risks: A case report describes acute kidney injury after combining it with ciclosporin. It is on the WADA prohibited list.

chain: Oral androgen binds the androgen receptor
Users report more muscle mass and strength
angle.text: Sold in supplements for bodybuilders, M1T is described by marketers and users as a muscle-building androgen. The published data are cell and rat experiments showing potent androgen receptor activity, plus case-level reports of harm.
